content: Surface energy is a measure of the disruption of intermolecular bonds that occurs when a surface is created. In the physics of solids, surfaces are inherently less energetically favorable than the bulk of the material. If this were not the case, there would be a driving force for surfaces to form, and the material would exist entirely as a surface, as seen in the process of sublimation. Surface energy is therefore defined as the excess energy present at the surface of a material compared to its bulk. For liquids, surface tension (force per unit length) and surface energy density are identical. However, in solids, surface energy and surface tension are not equivalent. When a solid is cut into pieces, the bonds within the material are disrupted, consuming energy. If this cutting process is performed reversibly, the energy consumed will equal the energy inherent in the two new surfaces created. The unit surface energy of a material is thus half of its cohesive energy, assuming all other factors remain constant. This is true only for surfaces freshly prepared in a vacuum. Surfaces often deviate from the simple cleaved bond model, as they are dynamic regions that can rearrange or react to reduce energy through processes such as passivation or adsorption. Measuring the Surface Energy of a Liquid Thomas Young, in 1805, described the interaction between cohesive forces (within the liquid) and adhesive forces (between the liquid and the surface) as the determinant of whether wetting occurs. Wetting refers to the spreading of a liquid over a surface. If complete wetting does not occur, the liquid forms a bead with a contact angle that depends on the surface energies of the system. Surface energy is commonly quantified using a contact angle goniometer and various methods. Young explained that surface energy is governed by the balance between cohesion and adhesion forces, which dictate whether a liquid drop spreads out flat or forms a bead. By measuring the contact angle where the drop meets the solid surface, the surface energies of the system can be determined. Young's Equation Young formulated an equation that defines the balance of forces caused by a wet drop on a dry surface. For hydrophobic surfaces, the contact angle of a water droplet is larger, while hydrophilicity is indicated by smaller contact angles and higher surface energy. Water, being polar and capable of forming hydrogen bonds, naturally has high surface energy. Young's equation relates the interfacial tensions between the solid and liquid, liquid and vapor, and solid and vapor, denoted as γ_SL, γ_LV, and γ_SV, respectively. The equilibrium contact angle (θ_c) of the drop on the surface is derived from these interfacial tensions. The equation assumes a perfectly flat surface, but in reality, surface roughness and impurities often cause deviations from the predicted equilibrium contact angle. Even on a smooth surface, a drop can exhibit a range of contact angles, from the advancing contact angle (θ_A) to the receding contact angle (θ_R). The equilibrium contact angle (θ_c) can be calculated using these values, as shown by Tadmor's derivation. In cases of dry wetting, the Young-Dupré equation is used, which incorporates the work of adhesion and accounts for the surface pressure of the liquid vapor, which can be significant. Pierre-Gilles de Gennes, a Nobel Prize laureate in physics, described the differences between wet and dry wetting, emphasizing the role of vapor saturation in these phenomena. Measuring the Surface Energy of a Solid The surface energy of a liquid can be measured by stretching a liquid membrane, which increases the surface area and, consequently, the surface energy density. However, this method is not applicable to solids because stretching a solid membrane induces elastic energy in the bulk in addition to increasing surface energy. The surface energy of a solid is typically measured at high temperatures, where the solid undergoes creep. At these temperatures, while the surface area changes, the volume remains approximately constant, allowing the surface energy density to be expressed. The surface energy density of a solid can be calculated by measuring parameters such as pressure (P), radius (r), and length (l) at equilibrium.
